title: Berdychiv to Callao: the Woman Who Denounced the Zwi Migdal
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Berdychiv, born in the Kiev Governorate
stops.date_confidence: attested; English and Spanish Wikipedia agree on 10 July 1900 and on the town, though one secondary summary of the trafficking historiography gives Lodz instead
stops.campa: She is born in Berdychiv, a town of the Kiev Governorate where the Jews are the majority and the market runs in Yiddish. The name written down for her that summer will pass through Polish, Yiddish and Spanish hands and come out differently each time: Ruchla Laja, Rokhl Lea, Rushla Laja, and at last the Raquel that Argentine paperwork will hand her. No street, no house, no synagogue register survives to fix the birth more exactly than the town itself. The empire counts her. Nothing else about the first years is written down.
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Berdychiv, Kiev Governorate, one of the largest Jewish towns of the Russian Empire

stops.name: Warsaw, the family moves west
stops.date_confidence: inferred; sources say only that she is still a child at the move and give no year, and no Warsaw address for the household is recorded anywhere reachable
stops.campa: The family leaves Berdychiv for Warsaw while she is still a child, and she grows up inside the Jewish quarter of a city that is Russian when they arrive and Polish before she marries. Nobody wrote down what she was taught or what trade her father kept, and no street is named for the household anywhere. She learns to sew. That skill enters the record only twenty years later and on another continent, at the moment it stops being enough to feed her children. Of the whole Warsaw childhood what survives is a city and a language.
suggested_refs: The Nalewki and Muranow Jewish quarter of Warsaw before the First World War

stops.name: Warsaw, the marriage to Jacobo Ferber
stops.date_confidence: year attested by both English and Spanish Wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: She marries Yaacov Ferber, called Jacobo in the Spanish records, a tailor, under Jewish religious rites. Neither the synagogue nor the witnesses are named in anything that survives; the wedding reaches the record only through what comes after it. Warsaw that year is newly the capital of a restored Poland, the war just ended and the Bolshevik army still to come. He has a trade and she has none. The household they set up is poor, and within two years he is asking what a passage to Buenos Aires costs for one man travelling alone.
suggested_refs: Jewish religious marriage registers of Warsaw, 1919

stops.name: Warsaw, the first son
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Spanish Wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: A son is born and is written down variously as Joshua, as Jose, and, two years later on a ship's manifest bound for Buenos Aires, as ICHIA. The accounts diverge on what the two boys are called: one pair of names gives Joshua and an unnamed brother, another gives Jose and Moises. The manifest, the only primary document in the whole case that anyone has produced, lists ICHIA and MOESCHE. No birth certificate for either boy has been found. Which of the five names his mother actually used for him in the house is not a question the record is able to take.
suggested_refs: The 1922 passenger manifest recording the sons as ICHIA and MOESCHE

stops.name: Warsaw, the second child and the husband's departure
stops.date_confidence: year attested; sources disagree on whether the second child is born before or after Ferber sails, and give no month
stops.campa: A second child is on the way, or already born, depending on which account is followed, when Ferber leaves for Argentina alone. The arrangement is the ordinary one for Jewish households of the Pale in these years: the man crosses first, finds work, saves the passage, sends for the rest. Thousands of families in Warsaw are divided on exactly this plan. Liberman stays behind with the boys for something over a year, in a city she will never see again, waiting for a letter with money in it.
suggested_refs: Chain migration of Polish Jewish families to Argentina, 1920s

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the husband lands first
stops.date_confidence: year narrated by English Wikipedia; no ship, no port of departure, and no exact date recorded for Ferber's crossing
stops.campa: Ferber comes off the boat at Retiro into the machinery every immigrant of the period meets: the sheds, the medical inspection, the registry clerks, the free lodging at the Hotel de Inmigrantes for those with nowhere to go. The port processes Italians, Spaniards, Syrians and Poles through the same doors and the same questions. Nothing distinguishes his arrival from tens of thousands of others that year. The record says he came, and that he came without his family. It says nothing else at all.
suggested_refs: The Hotel de Inmigrantes, Av. Antartida Argentina 1355, Retiro

stops.name: Tapalque, the tailor settles in the pampas
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; English Wikipedia places Ferber in Tapalque before his family arrives but gives no date for the move inland
stops.campa: He does not stay in the capital. He goes some three hundred kilometres inland to Tapalque, a small town on the pampas, and takes up his needle there among people who are not Jews and do not speak Yiddish. A tailor can work anywhere there are men who wear trousers. The fare for a wife and two sons has to come out of a small town's hems and cuffs, and it takes him the better part of a year to send it. He is preparing a household for a family still in Warsaw. He has about eighteen months to live.
suggested_refs: Tapalque, Buenos Aires Province, in the 1920s

stops.name: Hamburg, the crossing east to west
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction only; no ship name and no port of embarkation for this crossing has been located, and Bremerhaven is as likely as Hamburg
stops.campa: Somewhere on the North Sea coast she boards with two small children and whatever the family owns that will fit. The emigrant halls of Hamburg and Bremerhaven handle the bulk of Polish and Russian Jewish departures for the River Plate in these years, feeding steerage decks by the thousand across five weeks of Atlantic. Which of the two halls she passed through has not been established, and neither has the ship, the company, or the fare. Even the coast here is a reconstruction, Bremerhaven being as likely as Hamburg. The crossing survives only in its result: a woman and two small children standing on a quay in Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The Ballinstadt emigrant halls at Veddel, Hamburg, and the Bremerhaven emigrant sheds
sources: General pattern of Polish Jewish emigration to Argentina, 1920s; no ship record located

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, arrival with the two boys
stops.date_confidence: attested; Spanish Wikipedia cites the ship manifest for 30 September 1922, English Wikipedia gives only the year, and a secondary summary giving 1918 has no document behind it
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of September she lands at Buenos Aires with two sons, aged two and one. The manifest that takes them down, the boys as ICHIA and MOESCHE and herself as the wife of a man waiting inland, is the only paper anyone has ever produced from her own life. It gives names, ages and a date, and it gives nothing further. Every claim made about her since, in courtrooms and novels and newspaper commemorations, is built on those three columns. She comes down the gangway at twenty-two, with no Spanish.
suggested_refs: The 30 September 1922 passenger manifest cited by Spanish Wikipedia

stops.name: Tapalque, the family reunited
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact and the year; the exact date of the family's reunion inland is not recorded
stops.campa: The family comes together in a pampas town with a Yiddish-speaking population of four. This is the whole of the settled, licit family life the record grants her in Argentina: a tailor's household, two toddlers, a language nobody outside the door speaks, wheat country to the horizon in every direction. Ferber has his needle and his customers. She keeps the house and the boys. She has crossed an ocean and six hundred kilometres of pampas to arrive here, and not a word is written down about the months that follow. It lasts less than a year.
suggested_refs: Jewish immigrant families in the interior towns of Buenos Aires Province

stops.name: Tapalque, the death of Jacobo Ferber
stops.date_confidence: Spanish Wikipedia specifies 1923; English Wikipedia says only that Ferber died shortly after the 1922 arrival, and no month is given by either
stops.campa: Ferber dies of tuberculosis in Tapalque. Liberman is twenty-two or twenty-three, a widow in a country she has been in for a few months, without Spanish, without income, without kin, with two children under four. The English account says only that he died soon after she landed; the Spanish account puts it in 1923. Neither describes the funeral, the burial, or who washed the body. Whether a single household in that town took her in for a week afterwards is a question no source has ever thought to ask.
suggested_refs: Tuberculosis mortality among immigrants in rural Buenos Aires Province, 1920s

stops.name: Tapalque, the sons left with a foster family
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact by both English and Spanish Wikipedia; the date is inferred from the sequence and no month is given
stops.campa: Sewing does not keep three people alive. She places the two boys with a foster family and takes the train for the capital to look for work, meaning to send money back and to send for them when she can. The family who takes them is not named, and no source records what she promised them or what the arrangement cost. Whether anyone in Tapalque tried to stop her is likewise unwritten. She is twenty-two, she has the sewing trade she learned in Warsaw, and she is going to a city of two million people whose language she does not speak.
suggested_refs: Foster arrangements for immigrant children in rural Argentina, 1920s

stops.name: Avellaneda, the Varsovia society is registered
stops.date_confidence: 1906 is the commonly cited date of legal registration; some sources trace the trafficking milieu itself back to the 1860s, and the month is not given
stops.campa: Seventeen years before Liberman reaches Argentina, in the industrial town then called Barracas al Sud, a trafficking network files papers as the Sociedad Israelita de Socorros Mutuos Varsovia, a Jewish mutual aid society. The registration is genuine. The society keeps books, holds meetings, elects officers, buries its dead. What it exists to do is buy and sell women, most of them Jewish women brought from Poland and the Pale. A legally constituted charity is not a thing the police of Buenos Aires go looking into. Those books stay open, and stay honest about the trade they record, for the next twenty-four years.
suggested_refs: The registration of the Sociedad Israelita de Socorros Mutuos Varsovia, Avellaneda

stops.name: Avenida Cordoba 3280, the house with a synagogue and a funeral parlour
stops.date_confidence: the building and its contents are attested by Spanish Wikipedia without a date; placed in the 1920s, the decade of the network's peak
stops.campa: The society runs its command from a two-storey building on Avenida Cordoba with a garden, a synagogue, a hall for parties, a bar, a dining room, and a room for laying out the dead. A member can be married in it, fed in it, and buried out of it. The men who own the brothels of Junin and Lavalle come here to vote on admissions and settle disputes over property, and the property in question is women. Minutes are taken at the meetings. The membership roll is kept in the house, written up and filed, alongside the deeds and the accounts.
suggested_refs: The Zwi Migdal headquarters at Av. Cordoba 3280, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, four hundred and thirty men
stops.date_confidence: attested as a peak figure for the 1920s by English Wikipedia; the specific year within the decade is a placement, not a source claim
stops.campa: At its height the society counts roughly four hundred and thirty members. Between them they hold something like two thousand brothels and four thousand trafficked women across the country. The arithmetic is nine or ten women to each man, and each man a shareholder in a registered charity. Members buy and sell houses among themselves and settle the accounts at the headquarters on Avenida Cordoba, under the elected officers, with minutes taken. The figures come from the organisation's own records and from the prosecutions that followed. No other census of the trade was ever taken.
suggested_refs: Membership rolls and brothel inventories of the Zwi Migdal seized in 1930

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the name Varsovia is given up
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia dates the Polish diplomatic complaint and the renaming to 1927, Spanish Wikipedia states that the Polish embassy complained in 1929; neither is preferred here
stops.campa: The government of Poland lodges a complaint: a criminal association in Buenos Aires is trading under the name of Warsaw. The society obliges and renames itself Zwi Migdal, after the member Luis Migdal, or, some say, for the sense of great force. One account dates the protest to 1927 and another to 1929. In twenty years of trading, this is the only formal objection any government has raised, and what it objects to is the name. The officers keep their posts. The houses keep their women. The books stay open to inspection under the new letterhead.
suggested_refs: Polish diplomatic correspondence objecting to the use of the name Varsovia

stops.name: Plaza Miserere, arriving in the city to look for work
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the neighbourhood; the sources record only that she came to Buenos Aires in 1923 seeking work, not where she first lodged
stops.campa: She comes into the capital at Once, the dense immigrant quarter around Plaza Miserere where the Yiddish signs are, because that is where a Polish Jewish widow with no Spanish would go. Where she lodged, whether she found sewing work at all, how long the money lasted: none of it is recorded. Somewhere in these streets in this year she meets, or is handed to, the men of the society. The gap between her getting off the train and her disappearance into their houses is a matter of months and contains no documented fact.
suggested_refs: The Once quarter around Plaza Miserere, centre of Jewish immigrant Buenos Aires

stops.name: Junin and Lavalle, taken by the network
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the mechanism is not, and Spanish Wikipedia sets out two competing versions without choosing between them
stops.campa: She comes under the control of a trafficker the sources name as Jaime Cissinger, or Jose Kissinger, the spelling shifting with the telling. How it was done is the point where the accounts split and stay split. One version has her taken outright. Another has her deceived by a promise of marriage or of respectable work. One line of the story puts the first contact back in Poland, before she ever sailed; another has it happen only after the widowhood. Both versions are in print. Neither has a document under it, and no source consulted has produced the trafficker's own name in a form two writers agree on.
suggested_refs: Recruitment methods of the Zwi Migdal in Poland and Argentina

stops.name: Cafe Parisien, the auctions on Avenida Alvear
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources and placed in the years of her captivity; the address given, avenida Alvear 3184, cannot be matched to any present street number, so this stop is pinned to the city centre rather than to a false address
stops.campa: The society holds its sales in a cafe on the avenida Alvear. Women newly landed are brought in and looked over, and members bid; the Spanish record calls the places where this happened the meat markets, and gives this one a street number, 3184. The street has since changed both its name and its numbering, so the room cannot now be stood in or photographed. No source claims Liberman was displayed in it, and nothing documents that she was. The men who did their bidding in it owned her.
suggested_refs: The Cafe Parisien, avenida Alvear 3184, named by Spanish Wikipedia as a Zwi Migdal auction site

stops.name: Hotel Palestina, the second sale room
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources; the hotel's address has not been located at all, so the stop is pinned to the city centre as a district marker
stops.campa: A second house, the Hotel Palestina, serves the same function: women displayed, members bidding, the sale entered among people who describe themselves in their own minutes as a benevolent society. Its address has not been located, which means the building either stands unmarked or does not stand. The market has premises, opening hours and prices, in a capital city with a police force and a daily press, and it runs for a quarter of a century. The police are paid. On the register it is a hotel.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Palestina, named by Spanish Wikipedia as a Zwi Migdal auction site

stops.name: Junin and Lavalle, the years no one can count
stops.date_confidence: the duration of her captivity is given three different ways in three places: at least four years in English Wikipedia, approximately six in Spanish Wikipedia's article on her, and eleven in Spanish Wikipedia's article on the Zwi Migdal
stops.campa: She is held in the brothels concentrated on Junin and Lavalle, in the same quarter where the Yiddish theatres and the kosher butchers are, a few blocks from the synagogues whose congregations refuse the traffickers burial and read them out of the community. How long she is held is written down three ways in three places: at least four years, about six years, eleven years. Seven years separate the shortest count from the longest, and no document exists that would decide between them.
suggested_refs: The brothel district at Junin and Lavalle, Balvanera

stops.name: Buenos Aires, buying herself out
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; neither English nor Spanish Wikipedia gives a year for the first escape, and the placement here follows only from a captivity beginning in 1923
stops.campa: She saves money without her owners knowing and buys her freedom out of the house, reportedly with a client's help. Nobody recorded how she hid the money, or what a woman's release cost, or who fixed the price. The year is not recorded either. The transaction is entirely ordinary within the society's own logic, which treats women as stock to be valued and transferred between members, and entirely unheard of in practice, because stock does not buy itself. She is somewhere past twenty-six years old.
suggested_refs: Practices of self-purchase and release within the Zwi Migdal system

stops.name: Calle Callao, the antique shop
stops.date_confidence: the shop is attested by both English and Spanish Wikipedia; the year is a reconstruction and the exact address on Callao is not preserved
stops.campa: She opens a small shop on Callao selling antiques and curios: a licit trade, a lease, a counter, a doorway with her own name behind it. It is the only interval of her adult life in Argentina in which she belongs to herself. The address has not survived, and nothing is recorded of what she sold, or whether the boys in Tapalque were ever sent for. A woman who buys her way out and then prospers in public is an argument the other four thousand can follow. The society's men come to the shop and warn her. Then they come back with a suitor.
suggested_refs: Calle Callao, Buenos Aires, site of Liberman's shop

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the marriage to Jose Salomon Korn
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by both English and Spanish Wikipedia; no month is given and the site of the ceremony is not recorded
stops.campa: A man courts her, proposes, and marries her under Jewish rites. His name is Jose Salomon Korn, he is a member of the society, and the whole courtship was commissioned. The ceremony is a fraud. He takes her savings and the shop with them and puts her back in a brothel. They did not simply seize her off the street; they spent months getting her consent first, so that the punishment would be legible to every other woman who might try the same escape. Both articles carry the marriage. Neither gives a date beyond the year.
suggested_refs: Jose Salomon Korn, Zwi Migdal member

stops.name: Junin and Lavalle, the second captivity
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact by English Wikipedia; no dates are given for the beginning or the length of the second confinement
stops.campa: She is back in the houses she bought her way out of, with nothing left of the years of saving, and the men who put her there are the same men, on the same two streets. Everything she will later tell the police she learns from the inside: the names on the rolls, the addresses, who owns which house, what the police are paid and by whom, which member sits on which committee at the house on Avenida Cordoba. She is held there through 1929, learning the organisation from inside its own houses.
suggested_refs: The Zwi Migdal brothels of Balvanera

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the second escape
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact by English Wikipedia; the date is inferred from its proximity to the 31 December denunciation, and no source describes how the escape was managed
stops.campa: She gets out a second time. Nothing at all is recorded about how: no account of the door, the hour, the money, the person who helped her, whether there was any such person at all. It is a complete blank in the middle of the story, and the story survives only because on the other side of it she walks into a police station instead of onto a train to Montevideo or a boat back to Europe. She has weeks of freedom in hand. Why she spent them this way is a question no source has ever answered.
suggested_refs: Escapes from Zwi Migdal houses, 1929

stops.name: Departamento Central de Policia, the complaint to Alsogaray
stops.date_confidence: the date 31 December 1929 is given by both English and Spanish Wikipedia; it does not appear in the underlying 2011 newspaper source, which dates only the denunciation to 1929
stops.campa: On the last day of the year she goes to the police and names the organisation. She chooses the commissioner Julio Alsogaray, who has the reputation inside the force of being the one man the society has not been able to buy, and she gives him what a hundred investigations never got: addresses, names, the working of the houses, told by someone who lived in them for six years. The society answers with flattery, then with offers, then with promises to kill her. She does not withdraw the complaint.
stops.quote: Solo se muere una vez, la denuncia no la retiro.
stops.quote_source: A line long attributed to her, first traceable to 'Reconocimiento a Raquel Liberman, pionera contra la trata de personas', diario El Argentino (Gualeguaychu), 21 November 2011, which reports it as hearsay ('dicen que dijo') and draws it from the fundamentos of a 2011 congressional initiative; no police or court document carrying these words has been located
suggested_refs: The Departamento Central de Policia, Moreno 1550, Buenos Aires
sources: diario El Argentino, 21 November 2011, via Internet Archive

stops.name: Palacio de Tribunales, the judge takes the case
stops.date_confidence: attested that Rodriguez Ocampo took the case in 1930 and ordered Alsogaray to investigate; the month is inferred from the sequence between the December complaint and the May raid
stops.campa: The investigating magistrate Manuel Rodriguez Ocampo takes up the file and orders Alsogaray to investigate. He is offered money, as everyone in the chain before him has been offered money, and he refuses it. Two men refusing bribes in the same case is what the whole thing turns on; the society's method for thirty years has been to buy the officials rather than hide from them, and this time the method fails twice in a row. The famous sentence attributed to the judge about the society threatening society itself cannot be traced to any document.
suggested_refs: The judicial file of Judge Manuel Rodriguez Ocampo, Buenos Aires, 1930

stops.name: Avenida Cordoba 3280, the raid on the headquarters
stops.date_confidence: attested; Spanish Wikipedia gives 30 May 1930 for the raid on the Zwi Migdal headquarters
stops.campa: The police go into the house on Avenida Cordoba and take the society's own papers: the membership rolls, the minutes, the property records, the whole apparatus of a charity that kept honest books about a dishonest trade. Everything needed to prosecute four hundred men has been sitting in a building with a synagogue in it, three kilometres from the courts, for twenty-four years, catalogued and kept in order by the men it incriminates. It is carried out to the street in boxes on the thirtieth of May.
suggested_refs: The seized membership rolls of the Zwi Migdal, 30 May 1930

stops.name: Palacio de Tribunales, the procesamiento of the hundred and eight
stops.date_confidence: attested; Spanish Wikipedia dates the procesamiento of 108 members to 27 September 1930, four months after the raid, and the two events are often wrongly reported as one
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of September the court orders a hundred and eight members of the society committed for trial. The Spanish record says procesamiento, which is indictment, not conviction, and the English retellings that turn the number into a hundred and eight convictions are describing something that did not happen. What did happen is that a hundred and eight men whom no Argentine court had ever touched were placed in the dock, on the testimony of one woman who had been their property.
suggested_refs: The procesamiento of 27 September 1930 against 108 members of the Zwi Migdal

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the three hundred and thirty-four warrants
stops.date_confidence: the figure of roughly 334 fugitives sought is attested by English Wikipedia; no precise date is given and the month here follows the September procesamiento
stops.campa: Beyond the men in custody the court seeks some three hundred and thirty-four more under warrant, on charges of criminal association and corruption. They are already gone, most of them across the river to Montevideo, some further. What the newspapers seize on is the scale: a national association with officers and a treasury, its whole membership named on a list the police did not have to compile. The warrants go out in October. The men they name are in Uruguay.
suggested_refs: Arrest warrants issued against Zwi Migdal fugitives, 1930

stops.name: Palacio de Tribunales, the appeal
stops.date_confidence: attested; English Wikipedia dates the releases to January 1931 and Spanish Wikipedia reports the appellate outcome without a month
stops.campa: The Camara de Apelaciones takes the case apart. The ground is that there is insufficient corroborating testimony beyond Liberman's own, which is true, because the other women will not come forward and the reason they will not is standing in the dock. The detainees are released in January. Of a hundred and eight men committed for trial, three are finally convicted, and they are the small ones. The owners go home. The Spanish record reports the reversal; the English retellings keep the hundred and eight and stop there.
suggested_refs: The judgment of the Camara de Apelaciones, Buenos Aires, January 1931

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the sons come back
stops.date_confidence: attested by Spanish Wikipedia that she was reunited with her two sons in her final years; the year is inferred and the household is not described anywhere
stops.campa: She gets her children back. They were two and one when she left them in Tapalque and they are ten and eleven now, and there is nothing in any source about what they had been told in the seven years between, what she told them, or whether they knew where she had been. Where the three of them lived is not recorded either, nor whether the foster family was paid. She has perhaps four years left. The ages of fourteen and fifteen commonly given for the boys at her death appear in no article that names a source; they are an arithmetic guess.
suggested_refs: Records of the Ferber sons in Buenos Aires after 1930

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the visa for Poland
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia states that she applied for a visa in 1934; no ticket, itinerary, or correspondence documenting the plan has been located, and the month is unknown
stops.campa: She applies for a visa to go back to Poland, apparently meaning to take the boys with her. There is no ticket in the record, no itinerary, no letter, no consular file that anyone has produced, only the application and the fact that the journey never happens. What she thought she was returning to, and whether anyone of hers was still alive there, is not written down. Warsaw in 1934 still has three hundred and fifty thousand Jews in it, and the quarter she grew up in has five more years to run.
suggested_refs: Polish consular visa records, Buenos Aires, 1934

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the diagnosis
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; both English and Spanish Wikipedia give thyroid cancer as the cause of death without dating the diagnosis, and the month here is a placement only
stops.campa: She is found to have cancer of the thyroid. Neither article says when it was found, who treated her, how it was treated, or how long she knew. The visa application and the illness fall in the same year and no source says which came first, so it cannot be told whether the plan to take her sons back to Poland was made by a woman who expected to live, or by one who had just been told she would not. Both readings have been printed. Neither is documented.
suggested_refs: Medical records of thyroid cancer treatment in Buenos Aires, 1934-1935

stops.name: Hospital Argerich, the death at thirty-four
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia gives 7 April 1935; Spanish Wikipedia contradicts itself, its infobox giving 7 April and its body text 17 April, and the Hospital Argerich detail comes from the Spanish material alone
stops.campa: Raquel Liberman dies of thyroid cancer at thirty-four, five years after the denunciation and four years after the men she named went home from the appeal. Her two sons are orphaned a second time. She has been in Argentina twelve years and seven months. Even the date is unsteady: one article gives the seventh of April 1935 in its own summary and the seventeenth in its own text, a few centimetres apart on the same page. No death certificate has been produced. The ten days stand unreconciled.
suggested_refs: Hospital Argerich, Barracas, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, no grave that anyone has found
stops.date_confidence: no burial record, cemetery, or monument has been located by any source consulted here; the date is the day after the death and stands for a burial that is not documented
stops.campa: Nobody has been able to say where she is buried. Searches on cemetery, tomb and burial return nothing: no plot, no stone, no communal register. Buenos Aires has Jewish cemeteries that keep careful books, and the society whose members those books refused to bury kept a funeral parlour of its own on Avenida Cordoba. Somewhere in that paperwork there is probably an entry for her. It has not been found. Where does the woman who broke the Zwi Migdal lie?
suggested_refs: Jewish communal burial registers of Buenos Aires, 1935
sources: Absence of results across English and Spanish Wikipedia and targeted burial searches

stops.name: Argentina, the society comes apart
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia describes the organisation as effectively ceasing to operate by 1939; the collapse is a process across the decade, not an event, and the single date here marks its end
stops.campa: Neither the convictions nor the cover held. What the trial destroyed was the society's standing as a charity: once the rolls were read into the record, no synagogue would take its money and no member could be buried as a respectable man. Hundreds of pimps are deported across the river to Uruguay through the thirties. By the end of the decade the organisation has effectively stopped operating. Some drift back in later years. The trade continues without a charter and without an address.
suggested_refs: Deportations of Zwi Migdal members to Uruguay in the 1930s

stops.name: Archivo General de la Nacion, a voice held only in transcripts
stops.date_confidence: not an event; the date is a placement for a source-critical stop about the state of the archive, which neither Wikipedia article dates
stops.campa: There is no diary, no letter, no memoir, no interview. Everything anyone has of her own words passes first through a police clerk taking a statement, then through a magistrate's questions, then through eighty years of retelling. The single sentence everybody quotes is traceable to a provincial newspaper of 2011, quoting a congressional commemoration, which reports it as something people say she said. She spoke for hours in that station on the last day of 1929. Not one line of it survives in her own words.
suggested_refs: Judicial and police files of the 1929-1931 Zwi Migdal case
sources: Absence of personal papers noted in English and Spanish Wikipedia
diario El Argentino, 21 November 2011, via Internet Archive

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Polaca and the novelists
stops.date_confidence: attested; Myrtha Schalom's novel is published in 2003 and reaches nine editions, and the other literary treatments are dated variously across the following two decades
stops.campa: Myrtha Schalom publishes La Polaca, a novel, and it runs to nine editions and becomes a one-woman play. Nora Glickman writes a study in English, Ilan Sheinfeld a novel, Talia Carner another, and Humberto Costantini leaves a Rapsodia de Raquel Liberman unfinished at his death. The interior life that circulates as her biography was written by these people, working seventy years after the fact. It had to be. The woman herself left a manifest, a complaint, and a death notice.
suggested_refs: Myrtha Schalom, La Polaca (2003); Nora Glickman, The Jewish White Slave Trade and the Untold Story of Raquel Liberman

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Premio Raquel Liberman
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 2010 by English Wikipedia; the day is not given and the building where the award was established is not recorded
stops.campa: The Argentine state creates an award in her name, the Premio Raquel Liberman, for work in defence of survivors of gender violence and of trafficking. Seventy-five years after her death, the state whose courts released the men she named puts her name on a medal handed to people doing what she did. Gabriela Bohm's half-hour documentary, Raquel: A Marked Woman, comes out of the same turn of attention. Most of what is now easy to find out about her at all dates from these years.
suggested_refs: The Premio Raquel Liberman, established June 2010

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a character on television
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 2019 telenovela contains a character based on her life; the actress commonly named for the role is not named by any source consulted here
stops.campa: The telenovela Argentina, tierra de amor y venganza puts a character based on her life into prime time, and several million people meet the Zwi Migdal for the first time through it. Which actress played the part is repeated everywhere and sourced nowhere; the Spanish article confirms only that the character exists, based on her life. Ninety years after the denunciation, several million viewers hold a version of her, and nobody watching has any way of telling which parts of it are hers.
suggested_refs: Argentina, tierra de amor y venganza (2019)

stops.name: Callao station, her name under Avenida Cordoba
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Spanish Wikipedia article on the station credits a vote of the city Legislature in 2023, while the Spanish article on Liberman gives 2019; English Wikipedia does not mention the station at all
stops.campa: The Buenos Aires Legislature renames the Callao station of Line D as Callao-Raquel Liberman. It stands under Avenida Cordoba between Callao and Rodriguez Pena, a few hundred metres from the street where she kept her antique shop, and along the same avenue, further west, where the society kept its synagogue and its funeral parlour at number 3280. The English-language record does not mention the station at all. Several thousand people a day read her name off the wall on their way to work.
